lessons: Hook lines that directly name a counter-intuitive or sensory conflict (e.g., pineapple eating you back, shark older than the US) correlate with high early retention above 1.8x at 10%, whereas empty or missing hooks show weaker performance.

Lines that explain technical chemical processes or slow mechanism breakdowns too early (e.g., specific cell structures or water displacement mechanics around 0.2-0.4 marks) consistently trigger the largest audience drop-offs.

Best-holding videos (such as the Greenland shark or Tuna vs Cod) maintain exceptionally high engagement past the 50% and end marks by establishing high-stakes biological anomalies rather than everyday kitchen trivia.
When a hook line is absent or generic (like in the onion or leaky eyes shorts), audience retention at 10% drops significantly compared to explicitly provocative hook lines.
worst_moment_types: Slow mechanical explanations of bodily reactions (e.g., dead skin cells swelling or internal volume loss)
Complex descriptions of cellular anatomy or enzyme storage locations midway through the short
Dry secondary context regarding everyday processes without an immediate narrative payoff
best_hook_types: Provocative statements about sensory experiences (e.g., 'Fresh pineapple is literally eating you back')
Extreme statistical or temporal claims about animals (e.g., 'This shark is older than the United States')
Direct contrast of physical appearances or material properties (e.g., tuna red meat vs cod white meat)
